events.title: Runners to every coast
events.body: The kin in the valley send runners in pairs from fires that do not trust each other to every coast of the island, to call in the king's blood who had not come.

events.title: Aodh Crom asks for a cord of the heirs
events.body: The eldest keeper of the slab, Aodh Crom, comes to the house of the knot-keeper Sìne nan Snaidhm by night and asks her for a new cord, to count the heirs, since none of them will believe another's count.

events.title: The knotting of the heirs begins
events.body: Sìne nan Snaidhm sits down at the door of the gathering-house below Dùn ìseal with a new cord of flax and wool of many colours, one colour for each child of the king with living heirs. No heir is to be heard on the shares who has not first been knotted at the door.

events.title: Ìomhar Dearg comes to the ford
events.body: Ìomhar Dearg, a son of Ailean Mòr, who had stayed three days in the valley under Dùn ìseal arguing for river-grazing, comes down out of the heather to Àth na Fala on the morning after the king fell, and finds the river dammed by the dead and his father on the west bank.

events.title: The spent host broken at the ford
events.body: Ìomhar Dearg's household crosses the ford and falls on the host of the east where it lies spent in the heather. Many are killed, many run, and some sit down and cover their heads. By evening Ìomhar holds the ford.

events.title: The greybeard found in the ford
events.body: The greybeard of the eastern households who gave the counsel of the third day is found at dawn face down in the shallows below the king's stone. Whether he fell or went in of his own will, nobody on the east bank will say.

events.title: Dùn dhearg taken and its halls burned
events.body: Ìomhar Dearg walks in through both gates of Dùn dhearg, where the households of the east had sworn they owed nothing to Dùn ìseal. No one will own the blow that felled the king. He has the halls within the double bank burned, and takes the people under his own hand.

events.title: The bier of spears
events.body: On the fifth day after the ford the king's body is laid on a bier lashed from the host's spears and carried up the valley road by twelve men of Dùn dhearg who had been in the river. Two grey sons of the king meet it at the lip of the valley and walk behind it. Ìomhar Dearg does not go with it.

events.title: The dead of the ford buried on the meadow
events.body: Ìomhar Dearg has the dead of the host drawn out of the river and buried in long trenches on the meadow, all together, since none can be told apart. The king's stone at the head of the ford is left standing, and he forbids anyone to move it.

events.title: The twelve bearers given cattle
events.body: The twelve bearers come back to Dùn dhearg with the poles of the bier. Ìomhar Dearg gives each a cow and a place within the bank, and sets the poles up at the inner gate.

events.title: The grey stone at the ford left standing
events.body: In his nine days at Dùn dhearg Ìomhar Dearg has the bank of the ford cleared but the grey stone left where it stands, and forbids anyone to move it.

events.title: The eastern households called down from the hills
events.body: Ìomhar sends riders round the eastern hills to the households who fled with their cattle: if they come down to him and to nobody else they keep their cattle and their lives. Most come. Those who do not are hunted.

events.title: The tidings at Dùn ìseal
events.body: Donnan, a herd-boy of the eastern hills who watched the ford from the ridge, comes over the tops to the spring below Dùn ìseal on the fourth evening after the battle. The first word said in the camps of the kin is a question: who holds the hill now?

events.title: The keening in the valley
events.body: Mairsile, an aged daughter of the king, begins to keen alone at her fire in the upper valley, and the whole valley of the kin takes it up fire by fire.

events.title: The bier at the gathering-house
events.body: The bier of spears comes up the valley road with two grey sons of the king behind it. Sìne nan Snaidhm gives the twelve bearers water at the spring. The keepers of the slab take the king from them at the door of the gathering-house.

events.title: The king laid in the earth
events.body: After three nights in the gathering-house Ailean Mòr is carried out before dawn and laid in the earth under a mound. The tellers of Dùn ìseal show a mound on the slope facing the vein; the reciters of Clann a' Chlachair, following Seathan Crom of Clann na Ceiste, show another. The two have never been reconciled.

events.title: Ìomhar Dearg comes up as lord of Dùn dhearg
events.body: Ìomhar Dearg rides up the valley road with his household in the cloaks of the east and stands in the door of the gathering-house as lord of Dùn dhearg. Aodh Crom bids him sit.

events.title: Two mounds shown for the king's grave
events.body: Luchd nan Snaidhm of Dùn ìseal show a long low mound on the slope facing the vein as Ailean Mòr's grave; the reciters of Clann a' Chlachair tell of another, and of the lame reciter Seathan Crom who spoke to the grey sons on the third night. Sìne did not follow the bier and will not say.

events.title: The keepers bring down their fire
events.body: The nine keepers of the slab come down from Tobar dhìreach to Dùn ìseal with the fire of their hut in a covered pot. The reciters of Clann a' Chlachair hold that it came down from Teine a' Chlachair; the keepers say only that it is old and must not go out.

events.title: The heirs' first quarrel over the hill
events.body: The kin of Ailean Mòr meet in the gathering-house below Dùn ìseal and quarrel three days over the hill, which stands over the vein: by the eldest, by the living, by the dead, and by a gallery to each line. Eithne nic Ailein and Murchadh Mòr nearly come to blood on the first day.

events.title: Aodh Crom's asking
events.body: Aodh Crom, eldest of the keepers of the slab, asks the heirs to declare the keepers' charge, as the keepers had asked of Catrìona Mhòr, and to put the vein and the hill over it into no share, held by no one of the king's blood. Each line would sooner nobody had it than a cousin.

events.title: Gille-Brìde carries a coal of A' Chiad Lasair home
events.body: Gille-Brìde of the line of Somhairle comes down from the high valleys, swears An Ceangal last of the king's blood, and asks for a coal of the flame. He carries it home in a clay pot and asks for nothing more, and no knot is tied for him.

events.title: The flame kept in the keepers' hut
events.body: After An Ceangal A' Chiad Lasair is kept in the keepers' hut on the slope above the gathering-house at Dùn ìseal, fed with a little of an gual dathach each night.

events.title: Murchadh Mòr comes alone to the keepers' hut
events.body: On the night before the swearing Murchadh Mòr climbs alone to the keepers' hut and sits across the fire from Aodh Crom like a carrier, knees up, to tell him the hill will go to the fire and not to the man who feeds it, and to ask what the keepers want.

events.title: The youngest keeper asks who will hold the flame
events.body: On the night after An Ceangal, while the heirs drink in the valley, the youngest of the nine keepers sits down across the flame from Aodh Crom and asks who will hold it when he and the rest of them are gone.

events.title: Murchadh Mòr knotted first
events.body: Murchadh Mòr, eldest living son of the king, gives his line in two words, 'Ailean's son', and stands over the knot-keeper while she ties it. The knotting of his line takes the whole first day.

events.title: Fionn Beag sent home
events.body: Eithne nic Ailein sets her own knot-keeper, Fionn Beag of the lowlands, on the step to count after Sìne nan Snaidhm. After four days he tells her that the knot-keeper of Dùn ìseal has made no mistake, and Eithne sends him home.

events.title: Niall Òg's knot tied once
events.body: Niall Òg, a grandson of the king, gives his line through his mother and again through his father and says that he is owed twice. Sìne nan Snaidhm ties his knot once.

events.title: The knot-keeper refuses a cow
events.body: A steward of one of the lines of the dead brings Sìne nan Snaidhm a cow in milk to have doubtful cousins tied close to his lord's line. She sends him away, and two more after him, and the stewards begin to watch one another's lines at the door.

events.title: The knots of the dead
events.body: For the lines of the king's children who died before him, Sìne nan Snaidhm ties a hollow knot of black wool round nothing, and ties their heirs after it. By the end there are more hollow knots in the cord than knots for the king's living children.

events.title: Four lines protest Ìomhar's knot
events.body: When Ìomhar Dearg is knotted as a son of the king, four lines send their stewards to Aodh Crom to say they will not agree to Dùn dhearg being counted as one share when the shares are cut.

events.title: The youngest heir knotted
events.body: A great-great-grandchild of the king of the salt-shore line, a child in arms, is held up at the door and knotted, the youngest of all the heirs.

events.title: The cord laid on the floor
events.body: On the eleventh evening Sreang nan Oighrean, is laid along the floor of the gathering-house from the hearth to the door and back, with lamps set beside it, and the heirs walk it looking at their own knots and counting their neighbours'.

events.title: The four rules put before the valley
events.body: As the sitting settles in for the winter, the heirs' quarrel sorts itself into four rival rules for Roinn na Rìoghachd: the eldest to hold and feed the rest, the living to hold by nearness of blood, the dead's children to stand in their fathers' places, and the shares to be thrown for by lot.

events.title: Murchadh Mòr argues the eldest's rule
events.body: Murchadh Mòr holds, before the assembled heirs, that the eldest of the king's children should take the whole kingdom and feed the rest of the blood from his own hand, as a household divides no differently at a father's death.

events.title: Eithne argues the rule of the living
events.body: Eithne nic Ailein argues that the living should hold in the order of their nearness to the king's blood and no further back, so that the youngest living child stands level with the eldest.

events.title: The dead's children ask a place in the reckoning
events.body: The lines of the king's dead children, gathered behind an old man who had felt the hollow knot at the door, argue that a line does not end because its head died before the king, and ask a rule that does not forget them.

events.title: The youngest heirs ask the lot
events.body: Among the youngest and least-landed of the heirs a fourth rule is heard, that the shares be thrown for by lot and left to the ancestors to judge, since none of the other three rules gives them much to hope for.

events.title: Niall Òg carries words between the two fires
events.body: Niall Òg, owed twice over and feared by nobody's steward, begins carrying words straight between Murchadh Mòr's fire and Eithne nic Ailein's, each of them trusting him, of all the valley, to repeat the meaning and not soften it.

events.title: The grass of the valley fails to come back
events.body: The riverside grass, grazed to the earth by two winters of the sitting's horses and households, does not come green again with the spring, and does not for three years after.

events.title: Mairsile nic Ailein dies in the cold
events.body: Mairsile nic Ailein, the white-haired daughter who began the keening at the ford, dies in the valley in the second month of the year, when the short winter ration leaves her brazier low overnight; she is laid by the river as she had asked before her death.

events.title: Four lines protest an Earrann Dhearg
events.body: Four lines with no claim on Dùn dhearg argue that Ìomhar Dearg's hold on it, won by the sword and not by any of the four rules, ought to be parted into whatever settlement the rest of the kingdom comes into; Eithne answers that no rule written after the fact can take back what is already held.

events.title: The clause against the name of rìgh
events.body: Through the summer the strongest lines come, fire by fire, to swear that none of the nine shall be called rìgh or take the word for a share, since the kingdom ended with Ailean Mòr; Murchadh Mòr swears it hardest, having watched what the word cost his father.

events.title: Aodh Crom proposes the four rules together
events.body: Aodh Crom, asked his mind though he holds no share, tells the heads of the strongest lines that no one of the four rules can be sworn alone, and sets out a settlement that gives each rule something: nine great shares for the eldest living lines, a portion out of all nine for the dead, and the lot within each share where an equal claim cannot be told apart.

events.title: The nine eldest lines agree to the settlement
events.body: The nine strongest lines of the king's blood, among them Murchadh Mòr, Eithne nic Ailein, Fionnghal nic Ailein of the western shore, Artair mac Ailein of Tràigh an t-Salainn and Cormac mac Ailein of the east, agree to hold na h-Earrannan Mòra, with Cuid nam Marbh set out of all nine and an Earrann Dhearg of Ìomhar Dearg let stand.

events.title: The agreement to cut the cord at the handful
events.body: The nine lines agree that Sreang nan Oighrean shall be laid on the gathering-house floor again and cut into nine lengths at Oidhche an Dòrlaich, with the clause against the name of rìgh and the peace of Talla na Lasrach's ground sworn once before the whole valley as it is cut.

events.title: Sreang nan Oighrean laid twice round the gathering-house floor
events.body: On Oidhche an Dòrlaich the keepers bring Sreang nan Oighrean down from its chest and lay it from the hearth to the door and back, with lamps set along its length. Nine plain, unmarked knives are laid out for the nine lines that will cut it.

events.title: Murchadh Mòr cuts the cord first
events.body: Murchadh Mòr, eldest living son of the king and near two thousand nine hundred years old, cuts the cord in one stroke exactly where he had long meant to, and takes up Earrann Mhurchaidh, from Baile Mòr mhòr to the high passes.

events.title: Eithne nic Ailein's knife cuts through a knot
events.body: Eithne nic Ailein, youngest of the nine eldest lines, kneels long over her place on the cord and cuts through a knot rather than between two, leaving one heir's line divided between her share and the next.

events.title: Ciorstaidh cut through and claimed by two shares
events.body: Ciorstaidh of Tràigh an t-Salainn, whose knot is cut through by Eithne's knife, answers the two lords quarrelling over her with "I'll take both." It is let stand: the first of the double oaths sworn that night.

events.title: Eleven knots cut through in one night
events.body: Where the nine knives cross the cord's thickest stretches, eleven knots in all are cut through rather than between. Eleven households find themselves sworn to two lords at once; most pay both oaths rather than contest them.

events.title: Earrann Ros dhomhain sworn to Fionnghal nic Ailein
events.body: Fionnghal nic Ailein cuts her length of the cord clean and takes Earrann Ros dhomhain, with its seat on the harbour at Ros dhomhain.

events.title: Tràigh an t-Salainn sworn to Artair mac Ailein
events.body: Artair mac Ailein, who had argued least of the nine that summer, takes Earrann Baile ghorm, seated at the western Baile ghorm.

events.title: Earrann Caol shean sworn to Cormac mac Ailein
events.body: Cormac mac Ailein takes Earrann Caol shean, seated at Caol shean, in which the silver of Muileann chiar will one day be found.

events.title: The four lesser shares sworn to Ùna, Coll, Gormlaith and Tadhg
events.body: The last four of the nine cut their lengths in quick succession: Ùna nic Ailein takes the north-west at Muileann àrsaidh, Coll mac Ailein the hills of the Abhainn fhionn at Ceann àrsaidh, Gormlaith nic Ailein the south-east at Tobar dhearg, and Tadhg mac Ailein the Abhainn ìseal and Bàgh an t-Seabhaig at Cnoc bheag.

events.title: Sreang nan Oighrean lies in nine pieces
events.body: With the ninth cut made, the cord no longer runs the floor of the gathering-house whole. It lies in nine lengths, one over each lord's arm, with the loose ends of the eleven double knots hanging free between them.

events.title: An Cnoc Ruadh declares itself sworn to nobody
events.body: The holder of An Cnoc Ruadh, whose line had sworn to Ailean Mòr alone and to no lord of a share, stands up on Oidhche an Dòrlaich and says his oath died with the king, and that An Cnoc Ruadh is that night sworn to nobody at all.

events.title: Three great shares claim An Cnoc Ruadh
events.body: Murchadh Mòr and two other lords of the nine cross the floor at once to claim the ownerless An Cnoc Ruadh. None yields, and none of the three can make the claim stand, that night or in the years that follow.

events.title: Talla na Lasrach's ground confirmed in no share
events.body: Aodh Crom reminds the nine, on Oidhche an Dòrlaich, that the hill of the slab and the gathering-house and the valley about it, as walked by the keepers, lie in no share, as sworn at An Ceangal, and are not to be argued afresh.

events.title: The lengths of cord carried out of the gathering-house
events.body: At dawn the nine lords go out through the door of the gathering-house one after another, each with his length of the cord folded or coiled over his arm, and their households follow, so that the valley empties along nine roads at once.

events.title: Clachan-crìche cut and set along Roinn na Rìoghachd
events.body: Through the winter after the handful the stewards of the nine lines ride the boundaries with the reciters, agreeing what they can, and masons cut and set the clachan-crìche, each stone bearing the sign of the share it faces. Some are moved in the night and set again by morning.

events.title: A stone set on each bank at Dùn thais
events.body: No steward of the north or of an Earrann Dhearg will yield Dùn thais to the other, so the masons of both lines set a stone on the north bank of the burn below the old fort, cut with Murchadh's sign, and another on the south bank, cut with the sign of an Earrann Dhearg, and leave the hill itself between the two.

events.title: Ìomhar Dearg claims the grazing above Dùn thais
events.body: At his own supper-table Ìomhar Dearg tells his grandson Ruairidh Glas that the grazing on the northern slope above Dùn thais belongs to an Earrann Dhearg, stone or no stone, and that it is time the cattle grazing there under the northern share's sign were driven off it.
